newsitem.title: CHINA: British universities still most popular in HK.
newsitem.headline: British universities still most popular in HK.

text.p: Hong Kong's handover to China may have fuelled a new patriotism but has done little to remove snobbish admiration of a British education in the former colony.
Six weeks into Chinese rule, hundreds of youngsters flocked to a British education fair on Thursday to apply for colleges and universities in the country of their former masters.
Bolstered by growing affluence and the prestige that still envelops a British education, many said they preferred to study in Britain rather than anywhere else.
This is despite a new wave of Chinese patriotism evident in the territory since the handover, and a heated debate over whether to make Hong Kong's own education more Chinese.
Secretary Lai Siu-chee, 45, who took a day off work to accompany her 17-year-old son to apply for a place in a college in London said a British education commands a premium.
"We've always thought British schools were more prestigious. Canada, for example, is so flooded with immigrants," she said.
"And being an ex-colony, we have closer links with Britain."
Super-capitalist Hong Kong, a British colony of 156 years, was handed back to China on July 1.
The annual fair featuring 88 institutions from across Britain attracted 660 students who came and asked questions and sought interviews in the first two hours of the three day event.
The organisers, the British Council, described the initial reception as very good and said they expect as many as 4,000 people to attend the fair.

"It's history, people opt to study in Britain because of the relationship between Britain and Hong Kong. They see it as prestigious," said Julia Leung, manager of the Education Counselling Service at The British Council in Hong Kong.
"Both education systems are also very similar and there is no need for any bridging courses, unlike in Canada or the United States," she told Reuters.
Competitive costs of living and tuition fees in Britain compared with popular destinations of study like the United States, Canada, Australia was another reason, Leung said.

Council data showed a swelling number of Hong Kong students enrolled on undergraduate and postgraduate courses in Britain in recent years. For the 1995/1996 academic year the number stood at 10,900, compared to 6,200 in 1993/1994.
Robin Halley, Schools Liaison officer at Queen Mary and Westfield College of the University of London, was surprised by Thursday's turnout.
"My feeling was that interest may have declined (with the sovereignty change)," Halley said. But he said the value people attached to a British education remained high.
For some, the reason was simple.
"I just want to improve my English," said Pandy Cheung, 18, who had just completed his British-style "A Level" school leaving exams and was now looking for a place at a British university.
